This happened during my second week at a new job, and it's honestly one of the most awkward things I've ever done.
My manager sent me a calendar invite for a team meeting at ten in the morning, and I clicked the link a few minutes early, like a good little employee trying to make a strong first impression.
The screen loaded, and I saw a bunch of faces I didn't recognize.
Not one of them looked familiar, but I figured, okay, maybe it's a bigger meeting than I thought, maybe some other departments joined too, or maybe it's a company-wide thing nobody told me about yet.
So I just sat there, camera off, waiting quietly for it to start.
A woman started talking about quarterly numbers for a company I had never heard of.
I mean, the name meant absolutely nothing to me.
But I thought, maybe this is some client, maybe my manager forgot to explain the full agenda when she sent the invite.
So I kept sitting there, nodding along to myself even though nobody could actually see me do it.
About ten minutes in, someone said a name that definitely wasn't anyone from my team.
And then someone else mentioned a product I had never heard of in my entire life.
That's when it finally hit me.
I was in the completely wrong meeting, and had been for almost ten full minutes.
I froze for a second, and then I panicked and just left the call without saying anything at all.
No goodbye, no explanation, nothing.
I just closed the tab like it never happened, like maybe if I acted fast enough, nobody would notice.
Then I checked my email, and turns out, I had clicked a link from an old job application I'd submitted months earlier.
The recruiter had accidentally sent me a generic company meeting link instead of the actual interview slot, and somehow it ended up sitting in my calendar this whole time.
I messaged my actual manager, completely embarrassed, and explained I'd joined the wrong call by mistake.

She laughed and said, "Well, at least you showed up early to something." Then she sent me the correct link, and I joined my real team meeting five minutes late, still a little shaken from the whole ordeal.
Later that day, I got an email from the first company.
It was from the woman who'd been talking about the numbers.
She wrote, "Not sure who joined us today, but welcome, whoever you are." I never replied, but honestly, I still think about that email sometimes.
Somewhere out there, a stranger still thinks I'm the most mysterious guest who ever joined their meeting.
